The vision of a Sashakt Bharat is being redefined. As geopolitical shifts, supply chain disruptions, technological breakthroughs and evolving energy dynamics continue to reshape the global landscape, national strength can no longer be measured solely by economic growth or resource availability. It is increasingly shaped by resilience, adaptability and the capability to anticipate change. As India advances towards its long-term development ambitions, the need is not merely to build a stronger nation, but to reimagine what strength itself means in an era of unprecedented transformation.

For India, this reimagined vision lies in building resilient infrastructure, securing critical resources, fostering innovation, accelerating industrial capabilities and building institutions that can thrive amid uncertainty. The aim is enhancing self-reliance while remaining globally connected, expanding opportunities while safeguarding stability, and shaping the foundations necessary to support the aspirations of a rapidly growing economy and society.
Reimagining Sashakt
Against this backdrop, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) continues to play a pivotal role in enabling national progress. As the energy landscape undergoes significant change, the Company is strengthening its core business, expanding its capabilities and pursuing new avenues of growth to enhance long-term competitiveness. Through investments in capacity, diversification, technology and operational excellence, HPCL is preparing itself to address emerging opportunities while contributing to India’s evolving development priorities.

The theme, “Reimagining Sashakt Bharat” reflects this broader vision of nation-building. It embodies a commitment to looking beyond conventional definitions of growth and embracing new possibilities that strengthen economic resilience, energy preparedness and future readiness. As India embarks on its next phase of development,, HPCL remains focused on supporting a nation that is not only stronger today, but better equipped for the opportunities and complexities of the future.
ABOUT THE REPORT
This Integrated Annual Report marks Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited’s (HPCL) third Integrated Report and presents a holistic overview of the company’s strategy, operational performance and value creation journey during FY 2025–26. The Report highlights how HPCL continues to strengthen its core businesses while advancing towards a more resilient, diversified and future-ready energy portfolio in a rapidly evolving global energy landscape. It provides insights into HPCL’s approach towards sustainable growth, operational excellence, stakeholder engagement and long-term value creation across financial and non-financial capitals.

The statutory and financial information presented in this Report has been prepared in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and the rules framed thereunder, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 and the applicable Secretarial Standards.

HPCL at a Glance
Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) is one of India’s leading integrated energy companies and a Maharatna Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE) under the administrative control of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Government of India.
As India’s leading marketer of industrial and automotive lubricants, HPCL continues to diversify its energy portfolio through investments in natural gas, biofuels, green hydrogen, electric mobility, and renewable energy. Guided by its Net Zero 2040 commitment, the Company is driving innovation, operational excellence, and sustainable growth while supporting India’s energy security and low-carbon transition.
The Company has established a strong presence across the entire downstream energy value chain, encompassing refining, petroleum marketing, LPG, lubricants, aviation fuels, pipelines, natural gas, and emerging clean energy businesses. Through an extensive nationwide infrastructure network, HPCL delivers reliable, safe, and sustainable energy solutions to millions of customers across India.

Sustainable Solutions for the Nation
HPCL offers a comprehensive portfolio of energy products and solutions, catering to the diverse requirements of retail, commercial, industrial, aviation, marine and institutional customers across India. Its offerings span transportation fuels, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), lubricants, bitumen, aviation turbine fuel, natural gas and other value-added energy solutions.

In line with the evolving energy landscape and India’s transition towards a low-carbon economy, HPCL continues to diversify its energy portfolio through investments in biofuels, compressed biogas (CBG), liquefied natural gas (LNG), green hydrogen, electric mobility infrastructure and renewable energy. Simultaneously, the Company is expanding its nationwide infrastructure, modernising refining and marketing assets, and leveraging digital technologies to enhance operational excellence and customer experience.
These strategic initiatives reinforce HPCL’s commitment to delivering safe, reliable, efficient and sustainable energy solutions while creating long-term value for stakeholders and contributing to India’s energy security and sustainable development.

CHAIRMAN’S MESSAGE
Realising the Dream of Sashakt Bharat
Dear Stakeholder(s),

Dear Stakeholder(s),
Today, as we stand on the threshold of a rapidly transforming energy landscape, we remain guided by HP FIRST values that have shaped our journey. These values continue to underpin our commitment to delivering energy responsibly, creating enduring stakeholder value and contributing meaningfully to India’s development.
It gives me immense pleasure to present the 74th Annual Report of your Company. As I complete my first full year in this esteemed Corporation, I am privileged to share HPCL’s performance, achievements and strategic progress during FY 2025-26.
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
Each milestone in this Annual Report tells a story. Every number represents collective efforts of our stakeholders whose commitment transforms vision into reality. Their dedication, perseverance and shared sense of purpose helped serve millions of customers across the length and breadth of India.
Your faith in HPCL inspires us to continually raise our aspirations, embrace new opportunities and build a stronger, more sustainable future together.
Navigating a Complex Economic Environment

Navigating a Complex Economic Environment
Our Stakeholder’s commitment to excellence made it possible to overcome every challenge and convert every opportunity into measurable success. The performance reflected is not merely the outcome of financial and operational achievements, but represents the spirit of One HPCL. One Purpose. This 74th Annual Report is, above all, a tribute to the people and partnerships that make this organisation what it is, and it is my privilege to share their story.
The 2025-26 fiscal cycle navigated intense turbulence in the global crude oil market, accentuated by a steep price spike in March 2026. This led to a shift in trade routes, driven by escalating geopolitical friction in West Asia. When supplies from the Strait of Hormuz stopped, our supply and operations teams worked round the clock so that not a single citizen was left waiting at a fuel pump or for supply of cooking gas cylinder. Volatility, we have come to learn, is not an interruption to our work—it is the very terrain on which we prove our worth.
As India’s GDP continues to grow at a strong rate of 7.7% in FY 2025-26, it reinforces its position as the world’s fastest- growing major economy. The energy sector continued to remain one of the major drivers contributing to India’s growth. On the global stage, India ranks as the world’s 3rd largest consumer of oil and primary energy.

The operating environment towards the close of the financial year was marked by heightened geopolitical uncertainties. During FY 2025-26, the Company aggressively diversified its energy supply chain by integrating 10 new grades into our crude basket. This strategic move elevates our total portfolio to a formidable 188 crude grades. Spot purchase of LPG during the year from outside Gulf countries strengthened diversification of otherwise concentrated LPG procurement from a particular region.
In this backdrop, FY 2025-26 marked another defining chapter in HPCL’s distinguished journey, one characterised by strategic progress in key initiatives and a steadfast commitment to nation-building. ‘Sashakt Bharat’ is not a slogan for us—it is a responsibility we carry to work each morning. As India aims for its rightful place among the largest economies, energy is the current that will carry it there, and HPCL intends to remain a reliable partner in that journey.
Specific measures for supply optimisation included nil imports of MS/HSD enabled by strategic sourcing from domestic refineries, cost takeout initiatives and improved coastal and rail logistics. These measures by our different teams boosted both supply chain resilience and enhanced logistical efficiency.

For over five decades, HPCL has evolved with India’s growth story, building a legacy founded on trust, innovation and excellence. As one of the country’s leading energy companies with a significant presence across refining, marketing and pipeline infrastructure, our progress reflects a relentless pursuit of value creation and operational leadership.
The supply chain disruptions were also proactively managed through flexible contractual structures and prudent inventory management. The integrated sourcing-to-marketing approach strongly positioned the company in a dynamic gas market.
As India advances towards its vision of becoming a developed economy, the energy sector has an increasingly critical role to play. Ensuring energy availability, affordability and sustainability will be central to supporting economic progress and improving quality of life for millions of citizens.
At the heart of this journey lies the trust and confidence of our stakeholders. I extend my sincere gratitude to our customers, shareholders, business partners and all stakeholders for their continued support.”
At HPCL, we remain deeply committed to this national agenda. Guided by our purpose of energising lives and enabling progress, we continued to strengthen our core businesses, invest in future-ready capabilities and create sustainable value for all stakeholders.

Refining Excellence
Refining continues to be one of HPCL’s strongest pillars of value creation. During FY 2025–26, our refineries processed a record crude throughput of 26.04 MMT. Capacity utilisation stood at 106.3%, reflecting sustained operational excellence and efficient asset management. Gross Refining Margin for the year stood at US$ 8.79 per barrel.
Our continued investments in technology, digitisation and process optimisation will ensure that HPCL’s refining assets remain globally competitive and future-ready.

Building the Gas and Alternate Energy Ecosystem
Natural gas is expected to play a critical role in India’s evolving energy mix. During FY 2025–26, HPCL strengthened its presence across the gas value chain through investments in LNG, City Gas Distribution and gas marketing infrastructure.
We also continued to invest in pipelines, LPG bottling plants, terminals, depots, Biofuels, logistics infrastructure and Renewables. During the year, capital expenditure amounted to ₹15,705 crore was made reflecting our commitment to building a future-ready energy ecosystem. These investments will strengthen energy accessibility while creating long-term value for stakeholders.

Our Natural gas portfolio expanded to 624 TMT, while the CGD segment recorded total sales (CNG+PNG) of 149 TMT. HPCL’s participation across multiple CGD entities continues to strengthen our position in India’s growing gas economy. Simultaneously, we continued to develop alternate energy infrastructure. The number of EV charging stations (including Battery Swapping Stations) installed across our retail network increased to 5,533 while CNG-enabled outlets reached 2,253 locations. These initiatives support our vision of becoming a diversified energy company capable of meeting evolving customer needs. And, when the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India dedicated our Chhara LNG Terminal to the nation, it marked more than the addition of an asset—it marked HPCL’s arrival in the LNG age.
Marketing Excellence: Serving a Growing Nation
HPCL’s marketing business delivered another year of strong performance, supported by expanding demand, customer- centric initiatives and an extensive distribution network. Total sales volume reached a record 51.45 MMT during the year. Retail sales stood at 30.83 MMT, while LPG sales reached 9.41 MMT.
Our retail network expanded by 1,351 outlets during the year, taking the total network to 25,098 outlets across the country. Simultaneously, we strengthened our non-fuel retailing initiatives and digital customer engagement platforms. HP

Innovation and Research-Led Growth
Advancing the Energy Transition
During the year, our R&D teams focused on refining technologies, process optimisation, sustainability solutions, biofuels and emerging energy opportunities. We filed 118 new patents during FY 2025–26, bringing the cumulative number of patent applications to 779 of which 66 patents were granted, bringing the total granted patents to 312.
The global transition towards cleaner energy presents both opportunities and responsibilities. I am often asked how an oil company should think about a cleaner future. My answer is simple: not as a threat to be managed, but as a chance to be earned. India is already ahead of its global commitments— and we intend to be among the builders of that future, not bystanders to it. At HPCL, we recognise that India’s transition pathway must balance the energy security, affordability and sustainability.
Your Company continues to foster a culture of innovation by collaborating with startups to develop advanced solutions across the oil and gas value chain. As of March 31, 2026, 28 startups have received support, with cumulative disbursements of approximately ₹28.6 crore. These initiatives reflect our commitment to advancing continuous innovation and improvement.

Accordingly, we are pursuing a diversified approach that combines conventional energy leadership with investments in emerging energy solutions.
During the year, renewable energy capacity increased to 241 MW, advancing our pipeline of solar and wind assets. Green hydrogen remains a key strategic focus area. During FY 2025–26, Green H2 Purchase Agreement (GHPA) was signed with OCIOR Green Fuels Pvt Ltd for supply of 5 KTPA to Visakh Refinery on a BOO basis. Some of the year’s most quietly remarkable work happened at the edges of what we believed is possible: at Visakh, we turned used cooking oil—the very kind discarded from household kitchens—into sustainable aviation fuel; and in our laboratories, we coaxed bio-crude from seaweed. Modest steps today, perhaps, but they are the seeds of the energy company we are determined to become.
Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, advanced analytics, machine learning and predictive maintenance are increasingly transforming the way we operate and create value. We remain committed to leveraging innovation to improve operational efficiency, strengthen sustainability and unlock new growth opportunities.
Accelerating Digital Transformation

Accelerating Digital Transformation
At HPCL, digital transformation is not merely a technology initiative; it is a business transformation programme designed to enhance agility, efficiency and customer-centricity. During FY 2025–26, we implemented several digital initiatives across refining, marketing and corporate functions.
To contribute to India’s energy self-reliance, we achieved 19.94% ethanol blending rate this year. Additionally, under the Government of India’s SATAT initiative to promote Compressed Biogas (CBG) as an alternative transport fuel, HPCL added three new CBG plants and increased the total CBG Plants under the SATAT scheme to 18. These efforts underscore our commitment to building a future-ready energy portfolio.
A Digital Transformation Roadmap is in place, with multiple projects completed and others ongoing. Advanced analytics platforms, enterprise-wide dashboards and automation solutions are enabling faster decision-making and improved business performance.
Sustainability at the Core
Today, every Strategic Business Unit is an active participant in HPCL’s digital transformation journey. By democratising the digital movement across the organisation, we have embedded digital thinking as a shared capability that is driving innovation, agility and sustainable growth.

GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK
Upholding Integrity, Strengthening Accountability, Enabling Sustainable Growth
HPCL conducts its business with the highest standards of integrity, transparency and accountability, guided by a robust corporate governance framework, well-defined internal policies and full compliance with applicable laws, regulations and statutory requirements. As a Maharatna Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE), the Company is subject to oversight by various regulatory and statutory authorities, including the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG), the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) and Parliamentary Committees, ensuring transparency and accountability in its operations.
HPCL remains committed to the Ten Principles of the United Nations Global Compact (UNGC) covering human rights, labour standards, environmental stewardship and anti-corruption. Through strong governance practices, effective risk management, ethical business conduct and responsible value chain management, the Company integrates sustainability and compliance into its decision-making processes, fostering stakeholder trust and creating sustainable long-term value.

ESG Governance

ESG Governance
A component of executive remuneration is linked to performance and is determined through a comprehensive evaluation of corporate performance, Strategic Business Unit (SBU) performance and individual achievements. The performance assessment framework incorporates a balanced scorecard comprising financial, operational, environmental, social and governance parameters relevant to the executive’s roles and responsibilities. This approach aligns executive performance with HPCL’s strategic objectives, promotes responsible business conduct and supports the creation of sustainable long-term value for all stakeholders.

Remuneration of Directors
The remuneration of HPCL’s Board-level executives and senior management is governed by the guidelines issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) for Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). As the nodal authority for CPSEs, the DPE prescribes policies relating to remuneration, performance evaluation, organisational autonomy, financial delegation and human resource management, thereby ensuring consistency, transparency and accountability across public sector enterprises.
In accordance with these guidelines, HPCL has established a structured remuneration framework comprising pay scales, allowances, performance-related pay, retirement benefits and other applicable compensation components for Board-level executives and senior management. The remuneration policy and any revisions thereto are considered and approved by the Board of Directors and, wherever required, are submitted to the Administrative Ministry for issuance of Presidential Directives.

Key Highlights
HPCL’s refining operations are anchored by two technologically advanced refineries located in Mumbai (9.5 MMTPA) and Visakhapatnam (15.0 MMTPA), providing the Company with a strong manufacturing base to meet the nation’s growing energy demand. Both the refineries produce BS-VI compliant fuels, supporting cleaner mobility, while the Mumbai Refinery also houses India’s largest lube refinery, with a Lube Oil Base Stock (LOBS) production capacity of 428 TMTPA, representing over 40% of the country’s installed LOBS capacity.

Operational Excellence

Operational Excellence
• Achieved the highest-ever aggregate crude throughput of 26.04 MMT during FY 2025–26, surpassing the previous record of 25.27 MMT in FY 2024–25. • Visakh Refinery recorded its highest-ever annual throughput of 16.04 MMT, while Mumbai Refinery processed 10.0 MMT, with both refineries operating at an average utilisation of 106.3% despite planned maintenance shutdowns. • Strong operational performance and optimisation initiatives led to record production of MS, HSD, LPG alongside achieving the distillate yield of 75.8 wt% during the year. Mumbai Refinery also achieved its lowest ever Fuel & Loss of 6.75 wt% during the year. • Processed 10 new crude grades during the year—the highest in a single year—expanding the crude basket to 188 grades and strengthening crude sourcing flexibility and feedstock optimisation.
The Company further strengthens its refining portfolio through strategic investments in key downstream joint ventures. HPCL holds a 48.993% stake in HPCL-Mittal Energy Limited (HMEL), which operates an 11.3 MMTPA refinery at Bathinda, Punjab, and a 16.955% stake in Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL), which has a refining capacity of 15.0 MMTPA.

HPCL is also developing the HPCL Rajasthan Refinery Limited (HRRL) project at Pachpadra, Barmer, in partnership with the Government of Rajasthan, with a 74% equity stake. Progressive commissioning of 9 MMTPA integrated grassroot Reﬁnery- cum-Petrochemical project at Balotra, Rajasthan (HRRL) is in progress. Crude is taken in CDU/VDU. This has facilitated the commencement of commissioning activities of secondary units in a sequential manner. Upon commissioning, HRRL will establish India’s first integrated greenfield refinery-cum-petrochemical complex, significantly enhancing the Company’s refining and petrochemical capabilities while supporting the country’s long- term energy and industrial growth.
Capacity Expansion and Refinery Modernisation

Capacity Expansion and Refinery Modernisation
• HPCL commissioned the Residue Upgradation Facility (RUF) at Visakh Refinery in December 2025, featuring the world’s first and largest LC Max unit with 3.55 MMTPA capacity, converting approximately 93% of bottom of the barrel residues into high value distillates and ranking among the most advanced facilities of its kind globally. • The RUF strengthens Visakh Refinery’s ability to process heavier and opportunity crudes while improving product quality and operational efficiency, and is equipped with DigiSuite, which delivers real time process insights and monitors catalyst performance and equipment health through advanced data analytics. • Visakh Refinery Modernisation Project (VRMP) units achieved design capacity, enhancing refinery complexity, product yields and operational efficiency. • Lube Modernisation & Bottom Upgradation Project is being taken up in Mumbai Refinery to increase the LOBS Production from current 475 KTPA to 764 KTPA and increase in Bitumen Production by approx. 487 KTPA, is progressing at good pace and has achieved significant milestones during the year.

Approach to Research & Development and Strategic Thrust Areas
Inovation and technology development remain key drivers of HPCL’s long term competitiveness and sustainable growth. The HP Green R&D Centre (HPGRDC) at Bengaluru serves as the cornerstone of the Company’s research, technology and innovation ecosystem, supporting advancements across refining, marketing, lubricants, petrochemicals, specialty products and emerging clean energy businesses.
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
HPCL’s research and innovation strategy is closely aligned with the Company’s long term vision of becoming a future ready, technology driven and self reliant integrated energy company. Through the HP Green R&D Centre (HPGRDC), the Company develops indigenous technologies, enhances operational efficiency, supports the energy transition and creates sustainable solutions that strengthen business competitiveness and long term value creation.

Spread across a state of the art green campus of approximately 5.6 lakh square feet, HPGRDC houses 24 specialised laboratories dedicated to frontier research in areas including fluid catalytic cracking (FCC), hydroprocessing, catalysis, bio processes, crude evaluation, petrochemicals and polymers, battery technologies, nanotechnology, hydrogen, solar energy, bitumen and pavement engineering. The Centre also hosts a dedicated Global Technology Centre, providing advanced technical support and process optimisation solutions for HPCL’s refinery operations.
HPGRDC’s research portfolio is organised around five strategic thrust areas, reflecting HPCL’s commitment to innovation, operational excellence and sustainable growth.

Technology Commercialisation and Scale-Up
Commercialisation of indigenous technologies is a key pillar of HPCL’s innovation strategy, enabling the Company to transform research outcomes into commercially viable solutions that enhance operational excellence, strengthen technological self- reliance and create long-term business value. By accelerating the deployment of home-grown technologies across refining, petrochemicals, clean energy and specialty products, HPCL continues to support the Government of India’s Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative while reinforcing its competitive advantage.
HP-COAT (Crude to Olefins & Aromatics Technology): HPCL completed the basic engineering package for the 80 KTPA HP-COAT Demonstration Unit at the Visakh Refinery. The project has reached the final stages of mechanical completion, while SprayMax FCC feed nozzles and FCC stripper packing, developed and fabricated in-house, were successfully delivered for implementation.

HP-DAK Technology: HPCL successfully commissioned the 52 KTPA HP-DAK Plant at its Mumbai Refinery, marking the commercial-scale deployment of this indigenously developed technology. The plant has demonstrated stable and sustained operations, validated the technology’s commercial viability while reinforced HPCL’s technological self-reliance, and operational excellence.
HP-PSA: Commercialisation of HPCL’s proprietary HP- PSA technology gained momentum through a strategic collaboration with Engineers India Limited (EIL). While EIL is actively pursuing commercial opportunities with potential customers, the MR-ROG PSA project at Mumbai Refinery is being jointly executed by HPCL and EIL, supporting the technology’s large-scale commercial deployment.
HP-COSOL: Since its deployment across all three Lube Solvent Extraction Units at the Mumbai Refinery in 2022, HP-COSOL has consistently delivered stable plant-scale performance.
HP-BH2 (CO2 Capture Technology): During FY 2025–26, HPCL commissioned a 24 KTPA CO2 capture demonstration unit at the Visakh Refinery based on HiGAS (Rotating Packed Bed) technology for carbon capture from Hydrogen Generation Unit (HGU) streams. The successful completion of the Mechanical Run Test (MRT) marked an important milestone towards technology validation and future commercial deployment, supporting HPCL’s carbon capture and decarbonisation initiatives.

HP-AEME (Green Hydrogen Electrolyser): HPGRDC successfully scaled up its proprietary Anion Exchange Membrane (AEM) Electrolyser technology to a 1 MW- equivalent cell size for performance validation and demonstration. With manufacturing partners engaged to support commercial-scale production, the technology is advancing towards deployment and is expected to strengthen HPCL’s capabilities in green hydrogen and next- generation electrolysis technologies.
HP-TDAE (Treated Distillate Aromatic Extract Technology): HPCL’s proprietary process for the production of environmentally compliant Treated Distillate Aromatic Extract (TDAE) rubber processing oils, low in Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAH), progressed towards commercialisation during FY 2025-26. The 48 KTPA plant at the Mumbai Refinery achieved mechanical completion and is being readied for commissioning.
HP-TriJet (Sustainable Aviation Fuel Technology): HPCL’s HP-TriJet technology converts Used Cooking Oil (UCO) into Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), renewable diesel and renewable naphtha. The Basic Design Engineering Package (BDEP) for the 7.4 KTPA demonstration unit at the Visakh Refinery was completed, with detailed engineering currently in progress, advancing the technology towards commercial deployment.

Product Scale-Up (PSU) Facility: HPGRDC’s dedicated Product Scale-Up facility is being used extensively to scale up in house developed chemicals and additives from laboratory to trial and demonstration volumes. During FY 2025-26, 10 products were scaled up to a total of approximately 18 MT for field trials and demonstrations, accelerating the pathway from research to commercial readiness.
HP-NTO (Naphtha-to-Olefins Technology): To accelerate the commercialisation of HP-NTO technology, HPCL entered into a Joint Development and Cooperation Agreement (JDCA) with Lummus Technology, USA.

Nine Locations Achieve Net Zero Operational Carbon Certification

Nine Locations Achieve Net Zero Operational Carbon Certification
The recognition was hard earned. The Net Zero certification, conducted by CII, followed a rigorous evaluation: a 12 month data review, comprehensive physical inspections, and assessment across policy and commitment, GHG emission inventory, action plans, mitigation strategies, sustenance measures and Scope 3 screening. By meeting the standard for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, SOD SBU has set a new industry benchmark and given HPCL’s 2040 commitment a proven, replicable template.
India’s Net Zero ambition for 2070 gives HPCL its horizon; the Corporation’s own roadmap to Net Zero for Scope 1 and Scope 2 operational carbon by 2040 sets the pace. In FY 2025 26, the Supply, Operations and Distribution(SOD) SBU turned that pledge into a national first.

India’s Net Zero ambition for 2070 gives HPCL its horizon; the Corporation’s own roadmap to Net Zero for Scope 1 and Scope 2 operational carbon by 2040 sets the pace. In FY 2025 26, the Supply, Operations and Distribution(SOD) SBU turned that pledge into a national first.
Through sustained decarbonisation measures and sustainable operating practices, SOD SBU achieved Net Zero Operational Carbon Certification at nine locations, making HPCL the first company in India to certify a Net Zero Operational Facility. The milestone was celebrated at the 14th GreenCo Summit 2025 in Hyderabad, held on the theme “Green Makes Business Sense” with the co theme “Beyond Commitments: Scaling Net Zero Action for 2030 and Beyond,” in the presence of Shri Duddilla Sridhar Babu, Honourable Minister for Information Technology, Electronics, Communications, Industries and Commerce, Government of Telangana, along with senior officials from the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII).

Directors’ Report
DEAR MEMBERS,
On behalf of the Board of Directors, it gives me immense pleasure in presenting this Report on the performance of your Corporation for the financial year ended March 31, 2026.
Financial Year 2025 - 26 has been a year of strong operational and marketing performance with stellar profitability of ₹ 17,175 Crore. The resilient refinery operations, sustained growth in market sales, healthy refining margins and continued progress in improving the company’s financial strengths, were hallmark achievements of your Corporation for the year. In this series, your Corporation achieved highest-ever refinery throughput of 26.04 million metric tonne (MMT) with an annual growth of 3.0%, and also the highest ever sales of 51.45 MMT, reflecting an impressive growth of 3.3% over the previous year.
The close of the year witnessed conflicts arising in Middle East leading to supply uncertainties and resultant volatility in the prices of Crude Oil and Petroleum Products in the international markets, and associated implications in the domestic market. These geopolitical developments are bound to have a pronounced impact on the Corporation, in the near future.

RUF was provided with “DigiSuite” to have real time process insights, catalyst and critical equipment condition using data analytics.

Risk Management Policy
The year marked a strategic inflection point, with Corporation’s major capital expenditure cycle nearing completion, including key projects such as the Visakh Refinery Residue Upgradation Facility (RUF). Your Corporation continued its investments in capital projects, largely funded through internal accruals, with residual long-term funding requirements being met through a judicious mix of instruments, including issuance of Non- Convertible Debentures (NCDs) and borrowings from the Oil Industry Development Board (OIDB) at highly competitive rates.

We operate in a dynamic environment which not only provides opportunities but also exposes the business to various internal and external risks. Your Corporation recognizes that all facets of its business involve significant risks and that its actions are increasingly exposed to greater scrutiny by the public, regulators, investors, and other stakeholders. To proactively identify and manage key risks for achieving our strategic objectives and enable the Corporation to deal with these enhanced business challenges and risks, an effective and pragmatic risk management framework has been institutionalized across the organization.
During the year, your Corporation also undertook strategic refinancing of existing long-term loans aggregating to ₹ 5,000 Crore (across INR and foreign currency), at more competitive interest rates, resulting in a reduction in finance costs. In addition, your Corporation facilitated interest cost optimization for its wholly owned subsidiary through refinancing of project loans, leading to improved finance costs at a consolidated level.

Your Corporation has fortified its Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework by incorporating the best practices recommended by internationally recognized standards such as COSO ERM 2017 and ISO 31000:2018. Our ERM Policy is periodically reviewed and encompasses a comprehensive array of risks that could impact our strategic objectives and overall performance. The objective is to integrate risk identification and management in the day-to-day operations of the business, wherein risk is continuously identified, assessed, monitored, graded and managed to an acceptable level. Your Corporation has engaged reputed external consultant to provide additional perspective and support the ERM processes.
In managing its short-term funding needs, your Corporation effectively leveraged a diversified mix of borrowing instruments to optimize its overall cost of borrowing. These included the Triparty Repo System (TREPS), Clearcorp Repo Order Matching System (CROMS), Buyers Credit, Revolving Line of Credit in USD, issuance of Commercial Paper, and other working capital facilities from banks.

A systematic process of periodic risk reviews is in place across all key Strategic Business Units (SBUs) and Functions. The Risk Management Committee meets periodically, at least twice in a financial year, to ensure that appropriate methodology, systems and processes are in place to review these risks as well as monitor the progress of implementation of various mitigation measures. The Board is also updated regularly on the risk review and mitigation measures of the identified risk.

Unspent CSR Account (UCSRA) for FY 2025-26: During FY 2025-26, HPCL allocated its CSR budget towards various projects and initiatives covered under Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013, focusing on key areas such as Child Care, Education, Health Care, Skill Development and other social development interventions. Against the allocated budget, an expenditure of ₹ 85.38 Crore was incurred during the year (excluding an amount of ₹ 6.99 Crore, set off from excess spent during previous financial year). The balance amount of ₹ 11.67 Crore pertains to milestone-based disbursements for ongoing multi-year projects, which are at various stages of implementation. In compliance with Section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the unspent amount was transferred to the Unspent CSR Account (UCSRA) on April 30, 2026 and shall be utilized in accordance with the applicable CSR Rules.

Status Update on Unspent CSR Account (UCSRA) for FY 2022-23: In compliance with statutory provisions, an amount of ₹ 58.74 Crore had been transferred to the designated Unspent CSR Account (UCSRA) for FY 2022-23 on April 28, 2023, towards eleven (11) projects, out of which ten (10) projects have been completed as per timelines (₹ 36.03 Crore in FY 2023-24 and ₹ 19.40 Crore in FY 2024-25). The project namely: ‘Construction of 2.2 MLD Water Treatment Plant, Indore, Madhya Pradesh’, with a total sanctioned amount of ₹ 3.30 Crore, to be implemented in coordination with the District Health Society, District Indore, Government of Madhya Pradesh could not be completed within the stipulated 3-year period, due to pending administrative approvals from external authorities. An amount of ₹ 0.83 Crore (specifically ₹ 82.67 lakh) was released to the implementing agency against a verified Utilization Certificate. The balance amount of ₹ 2.48 Crore towards the project, out of total project amount of ₹ 3.30 Crore transferred to said Bank Account, could not be spent by implementing agency, and thus, was not released by Corporation to the agency. Accordingly, in compliance with the statutory provisions of Section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the said unspent project balance of ₹ 2.48 Crore was permanently transferred out of the Unspent CSR Account (UCSRA) for FY 2022-23 to the Prime Minister’s National Relief Fund (PMNRF) on 29-04-2026. Accordingly, the UCSRA for FY 2022-23 has been fully utilized/settled.

Philosophy on Corporate Governance
At HPCL, Corporate Governance is to meet the Stakeholders aspirations and Societal expectations. The key principles on which this edifice is built includes well developed internal controls, systems and processes, transparency in business operations, performance and financial position, clearly defined management performance & accountability and full adherence to compliances and disclosures.
The Board of the Company constantly endeavours to set new goals and targets that complement the vision & mission of the Company so that the interests of stakeholders are protected.

Being a Government Company and in accordance with the provisions of Articles of Association of the Company, all the Directors on the Board are appointed by the Government of India (“GoI”) through Administrative Ministry i.e. Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas (“MOP&NG”).
This is made possible due to its well-defined Policy framework which includes Code of Conduct for Directors and Senior Management Personnel, Integrity Pact to enhance transparency in business operations, Public Grievance Redressal Mechanism, Whistleblower Policy, Empowerment and Authority Manual and the Procurement Manual.
The Chairman and Managing Director and other Whole Time Directors are generally appointed for a period of five years from the date of their assuming charge or till the date of their superannuation or until further orders from the GoI, whichever is earlier. Government Nominee Directors continue on the Board at the discretion of the Nominating authority or till ceasing to be officials of such nominating authority.

Being a Government Company, its activities are reviewed by several external authorities like the Comptroller & Auditor General of India (“C&AG”), the Central Vigilance Commission (“CVC”), Parliamentary Committees etc. The Annual Report on the affairs and working of the Company along with comments of C&AG is also placed regularly in both the Houses of Parliament.

6. Right to Information Act, 2005:
In compliance with the provisions of Regulation 17(5)(a) of the SEBI LODR, 2015 “Code of conduct for Board Members and Senior Management Personnel of Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited” has been devised by the Company including the duties of Independent Directors as envisaged in Regulation 17 (5) (b) of the SEBI LODR, 2015.

HPCL being a Public Authority is under the statutory obligation to comply with the provisions of the Right to Information Act, 2005 and therefore has a structured mechanism in place to deal with matters related to the RTI Act, and has also aligned to the Online RTI portal of DoPT, Government of India. All RTI applications/ first appeals received through the portal are handled through the portal itself, including the physical applications received offline. The mandatory reports such as Quarterly/ Annual reports are submitted periodically within the stipulated timelines on to the website of the Central Information Commission https://cic.gov.in/ . Further, as required under the said Act, all the relevant details and information mandated vide suo-motu disclosures under Section 4 (1) (b) are being regularly updated and hosted on the company’s corporate website www.hindustanpetroleum.com for the purpose of transparency and better understanding to the public at large.
The purpose of this Code is to enhance further ethical and transparent process in managing the affairs of the Company. This Code has been made applicable to:
1. All Whole-Time Directors;

3. Senior Management Personnel.

The Shares Department carries various activities in-house such as: Compliances under Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority (Accounting, Audit, Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016 (“IEPF Rules”), Dividend Reconciliation, Dividend Audits, Filing on-line Statutory Compliances on BSE Limited (“BSE”)/National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE”), TDS on Dividend and responding to grievances of shareholders received through Statutory bodies.

During the Financial Year 2025-26, HPCL has successfully handled and processed 3,474 Nos RTI applications, 564 Nos First Appeals and 64 Nos Second appeals (Hearing Notices from Hon’ble Central Information Commissioner). A. BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT Global Economy
Indian Economy
The provisional real GDP growth of 7.7% in FY 2025–26, with FY 2022–23 as the new base year, reflects the economy’s resilience amid persistent global trade uncertainties. The economy has demonstrated sustained momentum, recording real GDP growth of 7.2% in FY 2023–24 and 7.1% in FY 2024– 25. Growth has been supported by strong domestic demand, ongoing tax reforms such as income tax and GST rationalisation, relatively benign crude oil prices, government impetus on capital expenditure, supportive monetary and financial policies and lower inflation rates.
According to the International Monetary Fund’s April 2026 World Economic Outlook, global output grew by 3.4% in CY 2025, consistent with the 3.4% growth observed in CY 2024, and is projected to moderate to 3.1% in CY 2026.
The moderation reflects offsetting forces. Headwinds from shifting trade policies are tempered by rising technology investment, particularly in artificial intelligence across North America and Asia. Growth continues to be underpinned by supportive fiscal and monetary policies, favourable financial conditions and private-sector adaptability.

International Crude Oil market

International Crude Oil market
Dated Brent crude oil prices opened FY 2025–26 at US$ 67.7 per barrel in April 2025 and averaged US$ 70.3 per barrel over the year, with sharp volatility through the final quarter. For the first three quarters, prices trended lower as the market focused on a looming supply surplus and weaker demand expectations driven by escalating U.S.–China trade tariffs. Production discipline by the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies (OPEC+) and geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe provided intermittent support, but rising non-OPEC+ output, led by the United States and Brazil, capped prices. Sentiment shifted decisively in Q4. A military escalation in West Asia in March 2026 led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz (through which approximately 20% of global oil trade transits), producing a supply shock that drove prices sharply higher and closed the year with extreme volatility.
Global electricity demand increased by 3% year-on-year in CY 2025, slowing from 4.4% the year before. While demand from electric vehicles (+38%) and data centres (+17%) grew rapidly, they represented only small portions of the overall electricity demand increase. The main drivers of growth remained industry, household appliances and commercial buildings (excluding data centres).
Indian Energy Scenario

Indian Energy Scenario
Energy Demand in India grew by 1.1% in CY 2025, which was among the lowest rates recorded in recent years. In CY 2025, electricity demand in India grew by 1.4% y-o-y, marking the weakest growth rate since at least 1972, excluding the decline seen in 2020 during the pandemic. The muted growth was largely driven by milder weather conditions, with fewer heatwaves in the summer and an early onset of the monsoon season, which eased cooling needs and reduced peak loads during the hottest months.

Dated Brent crude oil prices declined in Q3 FY 2025–26, averaging US$ 63.7 per barrel compared with US$ 69.1 per barrel in Q2. Prices fell to US$ 64.8 per barrel in October 2025 as new U.S. tariffs on Chinese imports dampened global demand expectations and logistical hurdles from sanctions impacted regional trade. Benchmark Refining Margins

Benchmark Refining Margins
Singapore benchmark refinery margins improved during FY 2025–26 as compared to the last financial year, averaging US$ 6.3 per barrel for the full year. While the first half of the year saw margins pressured by rising global refinery runs and a firm Dubai crude oil price, the latter half experienced a significant uplift. The primary driver for this annual strength was the substantial widening of middle distillate cracks in Q3 and Q4, fuelled by winter heating demand and an acute geopolitical risk premium following military conflicts in the Middle East. Despite persistent weakness in Naphtha and a mid-year correction in Fuel Oil, the sharp spike in Gasoil margins toward the end of the year, triggered by supply shock concerns, ensured that overall refinery profitability remained robust compared to the previous financial year.

Dated Brent crude oil prices rose sharply during fourth quarter of FY 2025–26, averaging US$ 80.6 per barrel compared with US$ 63.7 per barrel in Q3. Prices remained relatively stable in January 2026 at US$ 66.8 per barrel and February 2026 at US$ 71.2 per barrel, as the market balanced a projected global supply surplus against persistent ‘war talk’ involving Iran. However, the market environment changed substantially in March 2026, with prices averaging US$ 103.9 per barrel. This surge was driven by an escalating military conflict between Iran, the U.S., and Israel, which led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. As this critical chokepoint handles nearly 20% of the world’s oil, the disruption caused a significant supply shock, sending prices briefly toward the US$ 130 per barrel mark. The benchmark for Middle Eastern high sulphur crude oil, Dubai crude oil price, even touched high of US$ 169 per barrel. This geopolitical crisis overshadowed fundamental surplus concerns, ending the financial year with extreme price volatility.

Singapore complex refining margins averaged US$ 5.6 per barrel during Q1 2025–26, marking a significant improvement from US$ 3.2 per barrel in Q4 2024–25 as refined product prices outpaced the rise in crude costs. The quarterly recovery was primarily driven by Gasoline margins, which rose to US$ 9.9 per barrel (up US$ 3.9 per barrel quarter-on-quarter) due to robust summer travel demand and tight inventories in the Atlantic Basin, and High Sulphur Fuel Oil 180 CST, which improved to US$ 1.8 per barrel from US$ -2.0 per barrel following a seasonal surge in Middle Eastern power generation demand. While Gasoil margins also strengthened to US$ 15.8 per barrel amid late- quarter geopolitical fears in the Middle East, Naphtha margins remained the weakest segment at US$ -4.6 per barrel as a sluggish petrochemical complex and a shift toward alternative feedstocks continued to weigh on the market.

Singapore complex refining margins averaged US$ 7.4 per barrel during Q3 FY 2025–26, rising from US$ 3.8 per barrel in the previous quarter as refined product prices outpaced crude benchmarks. The primary driver for this growth was the substantial strengthening of middle distillate cracks, which saw Gasoil margins climb to US$ 24.5 per barrel (higher by US$ 5.8 per barrel quarter-on-quarter) due to a heightened geopolitical risk premium and a seasonal surge in winter heating demand. Gasoline margins also provided significant support, rising to US$ 13.4 per barrel (higher by US$ 5.0 per barrel quarter-on-quarter) as a series of planned and unplanned refinery outages in the region tightened supplies. While Naphtha margins showed a slight recovery to US$ -3.2 per barrel as regional maintenance limited availability, the overall gains were partially offset by High Sulphur Fuel Oil 180 CST margins, which softened to US$ -7.0 per barrel (lower by US$ 1.5 per barrel quarter-on-quarter) as summer cooling demand in the Middle East ended and global supply balances lengthened.

Singapore complex refining margins averaged US$ 8.78 per barrel during Q4 FY 2025–26, remaining firm compared to the previous quarter as product strength, particularly in late Q4, successfully counteracted extreme crude price volatility. The quarterly performance was heavily back-loaded, with the majority of the strength materialising in March 2026 as middle distillate cracks surged. Gasoil margins averaged US$ 35.4 per barrel, reaching record highs as the West Asia conflict and closure of the Strait of Hormuz triggered acute fears of diesel supply deficits, particularly for Europe-bound flows. While Gasoline margins softened to US$ 5.6 per barrel (lower by US$ 7.8 per barrel quarter-on-quarter) due to persistent regional length and trade frictions earlier in the quarter, Naphtha margins also faced renewed pressure, falling to US$ -6.0 per barrel amid high feedstock costs. Similarly, High Sulphur Fuel Oil 180 CST margins weakened to US$ -8.1 per barrel as the market focused on potential bunker demand destruction caused by the geopolitical crisis. Ultimately, the significant spike in middle distillates toward the end of the financial year was the primary driver that sustained Singapore refining profitability through the supply shock.
Domestic Petroleum Products Consumption

Domestic Petroleum Products Consumption
India’s petroleum product consumption sustained its upward momentum in FY 2025–26, increasing by 1.7% to 243.2 MMT from 239.2 MMT in the previous year. The demand landscape during the year was shaped by robust industrial activity, expanding infrastructure and a surge in the aviation sector. The fiscal year was also marked by significant price fluctuations in the Indian Basket of Crude, which saw a sharp increase in early 2026 due to geopolitical tensions in West Asia.
The primary drivers of growth were the three key petroleum products — Petrol (MS), Diesel (HSD) and LPG. MS consumption maintained its strong upward trajectory, reaching a new high of 42.6 MMT, registering an impressive 6.5% growth, supported by rising automobile sales and increased mobility. HSD, accounting for nearly 39% of total consumption, grew by 3.6% to 94.7 MMT, reflecting sustained momentum in infrastructure development, freight movement, and overall economic activity. LPG consumption also continued its steady growth, increasing by 6% to 33.2 MMT, driven by household and industrial demand; however, growth in the latter half of the year faced competition from the expanding Piped Natural Gas (PNG) network in urban areas.

The outlook for global oil demand is forecast to rise by approximately 1.4 million barrels per day (mb/d) year-on-year in 2026, reaching an average of approximately 106.5 mb/d. The above demand will be driven almost entirely by non-OECD regions, mainly China, India, and Other Asia. Factors driving global energy demand are shifting. Demographic influences are waning as population growth slows. The share of the cement, iron, and steel industries in global energy demand growth is declining, while the share of industries such as plastics and manufacturing is expanding. Space cooling is a key demand driver as temperatures rise, especially in emerging economies with rising incomes. Structural changes in economies and the emergence of new demand drivers, such as AI and clean-technology manufacturing, are driving up energy consumption in specific industrial subsectors. Emerging sources of electricity demand, such as electric vehicles, heat pumps and highly concentrated loads like data centres, are expected to grow rapidly. Furthermore, total electricity generation from renewables is overtaking that from coal. Together, renewables and nuclear are expected to account for around half of global electricity generation by 2030.

C. STRATEGY
HPCL’s strategy takes a balanced and pragmatic approach to the evolving energy landscape. The Corporation continues to strengthen its core business in traditional fuels, ensuring security, affordability and supply reliability for India’s growing needs. In parallel, it is reducing the carbon intensity of refining operations through residue upgradation, fuel substitution (green hydrogen replacing grey hydrogen), electrification and renewable integration. The Corporation is also accelerating investments in emerging and alternate fuels, including biofuels, LNG, EV charging infrastructure and green hydrogen. During the year, as part of its green initiative, HPCL awarded a work order for a 5 KTA green hydrogen project at its Visakh Refinery.
The LNG import and regasification terminal of HPCL LNG Limited (HPLNG), a wholly owned subsidiary of HPCL, at Chhara Port in Gujarat is now operational. An MoU was signed with the Indian Gas Exchange (IGX) to list spare LNG storage capacity slots (both quantity- and period-based), enhancing commercial flexibility and secondary-market participation. This is in addition to term LNG contracts secured for supply continuity for captive consumption.

HPCL’s wholly owned subsidiary for green businesses, HP Renewable and Green Energy Limited (HPRGE), is operational and consolidating various opportunities. Two Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG) plants have been set up and another 24 are in various stages of execution. HPCL continues to leverage its network of over 25,000 retail outlets to develop the electric vehicle (EV) ecosystem in collaboration with technology start-ups, alongside forays into non-fuel businesses.
This dual-track approach allows HPCL to meet today’s demand efficiently while positioning the Corporation as a leader in the energy transition, aligned to market shifts and the evolving expectations of customers, regulators and investors.
Infrastructure augmentation strengthened supply resilience by commissioning the 80 TMT LPG cavern at Mangalore in 2025–26. Further, the 201 km Haldia– Panagarh LPG Pipeline is at an advanced stage of completion to cater to LPG demand in West Bengal, Bihar, and Jharkhand, while the 540 km Visakh–Raipur Pipeline project is progressing across Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Chhattisgarh to strengthen product evacuation from Visakh Refinery and enhance onward regional supply logistics through rail/road.
HPCL is also leveraging its R&D infrastructure at HP Green R&D Centre (HPGRDC) to develop products and technologies for the energy transition.

HPCL commissioned the Residue Upgradation Facility (RUF) at Visakh Refinery in December 2025, featuring the world’s first and largest LC-Max unit. With 3.55 MMTPA of capacity, the LC-Max–based RUF enables approximately 93% conversion of bottom-of-the-barrel residues into high-value distillates and is among the most advanced facilities of its kind globally. The unit enhances the refinery’s ability to process heavier and opportunity crudes while improving product quality and operational efficiency. The RUF is equipped with DigiSuite, which provides real-time process insights and monitors catalyst performance and equipment health through advanced data analytics.

• Evaluating the Company’s process for identification of lease contracts.

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting
A Company's internal financial control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company's internal financial control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the Company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the Company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the Company's assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.
Auditors’ Responsibility

Auditors’ Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company's internal financial controls with reference to standalone financial statements of the Company based on our audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with the Guidance Note issued by the ICAI and the Standards on Auditing prescribed under Section 143(10) of the Act, to the extent applicable to an audit of internal financial controls. Those Standards and the Guidance Note require that we comply with ethical requirements and plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether adequate internal financial controls with reference to standalone financial statements were established and maintained and if such controls operated effectively in all material respects.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting

Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls over financial reporting, including the possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial controls over financial reporting to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial control over financial reporting may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.

Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited referred to as “HPCL” or “the Corporation” was incorporated on 5th July, 1952. HPCL is a Government of India Enterprise listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange Limited and National Stock Exchange of India Limited, with Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (“ONGC” or “the Holding Company”) holding 54.90% as of March 31, 2026 (54.90% as of March 31, 2025). The Corporation is engaged, primarily in the business of refining of crude oil and marketing of petroleum products. The Corporation has, among others, refineries at Mumbai and Vishakhapatnam, LPG bottling plants and Lube blending plants. The Corporation’s marketing infrastructure includes vast network of Installations, Depots, Aviation Service Stations, Retail Outlets and LPG distributors.

40.A. Risk management framework

40.A. Risk management framework
The Corporation has established an Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework under the Corporation’s Enterprise Risk Management Charter and Policy, which is embedded at the forefront of business strategies and focuses on the stronger, deeper and trust-based relationship with the stakeholders. This framework provides necessary support to the business to navigate through the evolving risk landscape through dynamic risk management approach that embraces disruption and enhances resiliency and builds trust.
The Corporation is regularly reviewing the identified and emerging risks and taking appropriate risk mitigation measures.
The Risk Management Committee (RMC), receives regular insights on risk exposures faced by the Corporation, thereby enabling it to provide inputs on prompt actions to be taken as well as monitor the actions taken. The Board is also updated regularly on the risk assessment and mitigation procedures.
Technology has been enabled to support the ERM processes with a focus on optimizing risk exposures and automation of risk reporting across the organization.
40.B. Corporation has identified financial risk and categorised them in three parts Viz. (i) Credit Risk, (ii) Liquidity Risk & (iii) Market Risk. Details regarding sources of risk in each such category and how Corporation manages the risk is explained in following notes

40.B.1 - Credit risk
Credit risk is the risk of financial loss to the Corporation if a customer or counterparty to a financial instrument fails to meet their contractual obligations. The risk arises principally from the Corporation’s Receivables from Customers and so also from Investment Securities. The risk is managed through credit approval, establishing credit limits and continuous monitoring of the creditworthiness of Customers to whom the Corporation extends credit terms in the normal course of business.
The maximum exposure to credit risk in case of all the financial instruments covered below is restricted to their respective carrying amount.
Note: Refer Note 61 regarding loans given to consumers under Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojna (PMUY).

40.B.2. Liquidity risk
Liquidity risk is the risk that the Corporation will not be able to meet its financial obligations as they become due. Corporation has a strong focus on effective management of its liquidity to ensure that all business and financial commitments are met on time. The Corporation has adequate borrowing limits in place duly approved by its Shareholders and Board. Corporation’s sources of liquidity includes operating cash flows, cash and cash equivalents, fund and non-fund based credit lines from banks and liquid investment portfolio. Corporation ensures that there is minimal concentration risk by diversifying its portfolio across instruments and counterparties. Cash and fund flow management is monitored daily in order to have smooth and continuous business operations.

(i) Financing arrangements
The Corporation has adequate fund and non-fund based lines from various banks. The Corporation has sufficient borrowing limits in place duly approved by its Shareholders and Board. 40.B.3.2 Interest rate risk

40.B.3.2 Interest rate risk
The Corporation has long-term foreign currency syndicated loans with floating rate of interest, which exposes the Corporation to cash flow interest rate risk. The borrowings at floating rate are denominated in USD. The Corporation manages its cash flow interest rate risk by using floating-to-fixed interest rate swaps. Under this, the Corporation agrees with other Parties to exchange at specified intervals (i.e. quarterly), the difference between fixed contract rates and floating rate interest amounts calculated by referring to the agreed notional principal amounts. The Corporation monitors the interest rate movement and manages the interest rate risk, based on the Corporation's Forex Risk Management Policy. The Corporation also has a Forex Risk Management Cell (FRMC) that actively reviews the forex and interest rate exposures. The Corporation does not use derivative financial instruments for trading or speculative purposes.

40.B.3.5 Derivatives & Hedging
The Corporation enters into derivative contracts for hedging purpose, to mitigate the commodity price risk on Highly probable forecast transactions and Currency Risk. The Corporation has applied Hedge Accounting on commodity derivative transactions and foreign exchange forward derivatives as per Ind AS 109 (Financial Instruments). Consequent to this a Mark to Market Debit / (Credit) amounting to ₹ 41.00 Crore [2024-25: ₹ (95.48) Crore] towards commodity derivative transactions, has been accounted in Other Comprehensive Income which will be recycled to Statement of Profit and Loss in subsequent period on settlement of respective contracts.
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements

Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
All these hedges are accounted for as Cash Flow Hedges.
Hedge Effectiveness
The Corporation has established a hedge ratio of 1:1 for the hedging relationship as the underlying risk of the commodity derivative contracts are identical to the hedged risk component. Hedge item and the hedging instruments have economic relationship as the terms of the commodity derivative contracts match with the terms of hedge items. Considering the economic relationship and characteristics of the hedging instrument being aligned to the hedged item, the fair value changes in the hedging instrument reasonably approximates the fair value changes in the hedged Item (in absolute amounts).
Source of Hedge Ineffectiveness
The Corporation has identified the following sources of hedge ineffectiveness w.r.t commodity derivative contracts which are not expected to be material as at date:
a. Counterparty Credit Risk impacting the fair value of the hedge instrument and hedge item.
b. Difference in the timing of the cash flows of the hedged items and the hedge instruments.
c. Different indexes used to hedge risk of the hedged item.
d. Changes to forecasted amounts of cash flows of hedged items and hedging instruments.

d. Changes to forecasted amounts of cash flows of hedged items and hedging instruments.
In case of foreign currency risk, the main source of hedge ineffectiveness is the effect of the counterparty and the Corporation’s own credit risk on the fair value of the hedge contracts, which is not reflected in the fair value of the hedged items. The effect of this is not expected to be material.
Disclosures of effects of Cash Flow Hedge Accounting
The Corporation has applied Hedge Accounting prospectively for the highly probable forecast transactions and foreign exchange forwards as stated above. Consequently, disclosure is made only for the transactions designated for Hedge Accounting.

In addition, HPCL and GAIL had paid ₹ 22.49 Crore each as Advance against Equity / Share application money (totalling to ₹ 44.98 Crore). On 20th August 2014, BGL allotted 2,24,87,500 shares on preferential basis to each of HPCL and GAIL towards the money paid earlier, leading to increase in Corporation’s shareholding to 49.97%. KSPL had challenged this allotment in the Company Law Board (CLB), Chennai Bench, which dismissed it on 14th September 2014. Against this, KSPL moved the High Court, Telangana, which did not stay the dismissal order of CLB. BGL has further allotted equity shares to HPCL, GAIL and KSPL during FY 2018-19. Further, pursuant to issuance of equity shares during FY 2019-20 to Andhra Pradesh Industrial Infrastructure Corporation Limited, against land allotted earlier, Corporation’s shareholding in BGL was reduced to 48.73%. Pending adjudication of the appeal by KSPL before the High Court, the shareholding was considered at 24.99% till 31st March 2020. However, taking all the facts into consideration, including receipt of dividend on the entire stake of 48.73% during financial year 2020-21 and the Articles of Associations of BGL, the shareholding was being considered as at 48.73%, effective financial year 2020-21. During the FY 2024-25, BGL had allotted 22,88,000 Shares of ₹ 10/- each to Telangana State Industrial Infrastructure Corporation for land allotted earlier, resulting into change in Corporation shareholding from 48.73% to 47.51%, effective FY 2024-25.

Pursuant to paragraph 57 of Ind AS 19, accounting by an entity for defined benefit plans, inter-alia, involves determining the amount of the net defined benefit liability (asset) which shall be adjusted for any effect of limiting a net defined benefit asset to the asset ceiling prescribed in paragraph 64. As per Para 64 of Ind AS 19, in case of surplus in a defined benefit plan, an entity shall measure the net defined benefit asset at the lower of actual surplus or the value of the assets ceiling determined using the discount rate. The asset ceiling is the present value of any economic benefits available in the form of refunds from the plan or reductions in future contributions to the plan. Further, paragraph 65 provides that a net defined benefit asset may arise where a defined benefit plan has been overfunded or where actuarial gains have arisen.

As per the provisions of the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, the Company has no right to the benefits either in the form of refund from the plan or lower future contribution to the plan towards the net surplus of ₹ 4.49 Crore (31.03.2025: ₹ 16.99 Crore) determined through actuarial valuation. Accordingly, Company has not recognised the surplus as an asset, as these pertain to the Provident Fund Trust and not to the Company.

I. Gratuity: i) Each employee rendering continuous service of 5 Years or more is entitled to receive gratuity amount equal to 15/26 of the eligible salary for every completed years of service subject to maximum of ₹ 0.20 crore at the time of separation from the Corporation. Besides the ceiling, gratuity increases by 25% whenever IDA rises by 50%. The long term employee benefit of Gratuity is administered through a Trust, established under the erstwhile Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. The Board of Trustees comprises of representatives from the Employer who are also plan participants in accordance with the plans regulation. The liability towards gratuity is funded with Life Insurance Companies.
 ii) Pursuant to notification of Code on Social Security during the year, Actuarial Valuation of (unfunded) Gratuity liability has been carried-out towards fixed-term associates with the Corporation as of 31.03.2026.

The statutory auditors appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India under section 139(5) are responsible for expressing opinion on the financial statements under section 143 of the Act based on independent audit in accordance with the standards on auditing prescribed under section 143(10) of the Act. This is stated to have been done by them vide their Audit Report dated 13 May 2026.
I, on behalf of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, have conducted a supplementary audit of the financial statements of Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited for the year ended 31 March 2026 under section 143(6)(a) of the Act. This supplementary audit has been carried out independently without access to the working papers of the statutory auditors and is limited primarily to inquiries of the statutory auditors and company personnel and a selective examination of some of the accounting records.

On the basis of my supplementary audit nothing significant has come to my knowledge which would give rise to any comment upon or supplement to statutory auditors’ report under section 143(6)(b) of the Act.

Opinion
Basis for Opinion
We have audited the accompanying Consolidated Financial Statements of Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (“the Holding Company”) and its subsidiaries (the Holding Company and subsidiaries together referred to as “the Group”), its associates and joint ventures, which comprise the consolidated Balance Sheet as at March 31, 2026, the consolidated Statement of Profit and Loss (including Other Comprehensive Income), the consolidated Statement of Changes in Equity and the consolidated Statement of Cash Flows for the year then ended and notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements, including material accounting policy information and other explanatory information (hereinafter referred to as “the consolidated financial statements”).

We conducted our audit in accordance with the Standards on Auditing (“SAs”) specified under section 143(10) of the Act. Our responsibilities under those Standards are further described in the “Auditors’ Responsibilities for the Audit of the Consolidated Financial Statements” section of our report. We are independent of the Group, its associates and joint ventures in accordance with the Code of Ethics issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (the “ICAI”) together with the ethical requirements that are relevant to our audit of the consolidated financial statements under the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder, and we have fulfilled our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with these requirements. We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion.

In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us and based on the consideration of reports of other auditors on separate financial statements and on the other financial information of the subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures, the aforesaid consolidated financial statements give the information required by the Companies Act, 2013 (‘the Act’) in the manner so required and give a true and fair view in conformity with the Indian Accounting Standards prescribed under section 133 of the Act read with the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 as amended (“Ind AS”) and accounting principles generally accepted in India, of the consolidated state of affairs of the Group, of its associates and joint ventures as at March 31, 2026, of its consolidated profit, consolidated total comprehensive income, consolidated changes in equity and consolidated cash flows for the year ended on that date.

1 Property, Plant and Equipment and Capital Work in Progress
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
• We performed an understanding and evaluation of the system of internal control processes over the projects and those included in capital work in progress, with reference to identification and testing of key controls;

• There are areas where management judgements impact the carrying value of the property, plant and equipment, intangible assets and their respective depreciation/ amortization rates. These include the decision to capitalise or expense costs, the annual asset life review, the timeliness of the capitalisation of assets and the use of management assumptions and estimates for the determination or the measurement and recognition criteria for assets retired from active use.
• We ensured adequacy of disclosures in the consolidated financial statements.
• We reviewed the judgements made by the management including the nature of underlying costs capitalized, determination of realizable value of the assets retired from active use, the appropriateness of useful lives applied in the calculation of depreciation/amortization, the useful lives of assets prescribed in Schedule II to the Act and the useful lives of certain assets as per the technical assessment of the management. We have found that the management has regularly reviewed aforesaid judgments and there are no material changes.

This has been determined as a key audit matter due to the significance of the capital expenditure during the year as compared to the existing block of Property, Plant and Equipment, the risk that the elements of costs that are eligible for capitalisation are not appropriately capitalised in accordance with the recognition criteria provided in Ind AS 16, and the complex nature of the project. 3 Computation of Expected Credit Loss (ECL) How the Key Audit matter was addressed
• We evaluated the methodology used for age-wise classification of trade receivables and assessed the key assumptions underlying the estimated probability of default. This evaluation includes verifying consistency with the Company’s historical default trends.
Trade receivables constitute a significant component of the total current assets of the Holding Company. At each reporting date, the Holding Company recognizes lifetime expected credit losses on these Trade receivables wherein we relied on Management’s estimates regarding probability of default rates linked to age-wise bucketing of the underlying assets. Given, the technical complexity in estimating the probability of default; this area is considered as a key audit matter. (Refer Note No. 13)

4 Inventories How the Key Audit matter was addressed
• We evaluated the inventory monitoring and control system and noted that the physical verification of inventories is done by the Management at reasonable intervals.
The verification and valuation of inventories by the holding company is a significant area that involves considerable management judgment in the application of accounting policies and estimation techniques. Since, these judgments have a significant impact on the amounts recognized in the Consolidated Financial Statements, we have identified this area as a key audit matter. (Refer Note No. 11)
• Our audit teams conducted physical verification of inventories on a sample basis at various locations. However, since physical verification at every location is not possible, in such cases we placed reliance on the physical verification procedures carried out by the Management.
• For inventories held at third-party locations, we relied on the Company’s system of record-keeping related to such inventories.
• We also tested, on a sample basis, the values used for determining net realisable value and cost of inventories, and verified their consistency with the inventory valuation records and related accounting entries.

5 Leases (Ind AS 116) How the Key Audit matter was addressed
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
• Evaluating the Holding Company’s process for identification of lease contracts.
The Holding Company has adopted Ind AS 116 - Leases, which requires recognition of right-of-use assets and corresponding lease liabilities for all applicable lease arrangements. The application of this standard involves significant judgments, including determination of the lease term (considering renewal and termination options), identification of lease and non-lease components, and discounting of lease liabilities.
• Testing a sample of lease agreements to assess whether they meet the definition of a lease under Ind AS 116.
• Assessing the reasonableness of key assumptions such as lease term and discount rate.
• Verifying the mathematical accuracy of lease liability and right-of-use asset calculations.

• Verifying the mathematical accuracy of lease liability and right-of-use asset calculations.
Given the materiality of lease balances and the significant management judgment involved in measurement and recognition, this area was considered as a key audit matter. (Refer Note No. 3 & 43)
